The near-term reality

Alternative energy sources such as electric and hydrogen propulsion hold promise, but they won’t be ready in the next 10 years to support global air traffic at scale. And while engine efficiency improvements, route optimisation and operational measures can deliver incremental gains, SAF is the scalable, near-term solution to reduce lifecycle aviation emissions without changing aircraft or infrastructure.

The focus is now on how industry, governments and customers can work together to build the supply, infrastructure and confidence needed to scale SAF.

Why it matters now

In that context, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) has become central to aviation’s approach to navigating the energy transition and more recently, SAF is being seen as a potential energy security vector since it can be produced in refineries from local feedstocks. SAF is central to the aviation industry’s decarbonisation strategy and the industry’s challenge is now how to scale that supply. While emissions at the wingtip are essentially the same as for conventional fuel, lifecycle savings of up to 80% make it the most effective near-term lever available today. As a drop in fuel, it is produced to the same exacting specifications as conventional jet fuel and is compatible with today’s aircraft and refuelling systems.

The industry has shifted away from looking at whether SAF is viable, to how it can be supplied reliably, affordably and at scale. This shift places emphasis not only on the fuel itself, but on wider capability: production, logistics, certification, infrastructure and customer support.

Growing SAF at scale

SAF mandates are still at an early stage, with volumes set at very low levels, but they are already giving the aviation sector a clearer signal to invest and scale supply. bp is working with trade bodies and government on pragmatic policy that can support this competitiveness. We are also making the most of the production routes available today, including HEFA and co-processing, while helping to develop a broader range of sustainable feedstocks and technology pathways for future supply.

We believe there are some key priorities that could help give the industry greater confidence to invest in SAF and help to scale production.

1. Long-term demand certainty

SAF mandates, such as those now in place in the EU and UK, help provide clarity for both producers and customers, support investment decisions and plan across the supply chain. The industry successfully scaled production to meet the EU’s 2% mandate in 2025 and is continuing to ramp up its output as the mandate thresholds increase. Consistent implementation of these mandates across other major aviation markets could further strengthen confidence across the industry.

However, the economics remain challenging. Government support will be essential to unlock financing, reduce project risk, and provide the long-term revenue certainty needed to scale production. The EU has set ambitious mandates for e-SAF, synthetic jet fuel made with renewable energy, which come into force in 2030 and look challenging for the industry to meet. The complexities of producing e-SAF mean that those that may have the capability to establish the first, experimental production facilities could face high costs, without the revenue certainty to support the necessary allocation of capital.

2. Scaling SAF requires access to a broader range of sustainable feedstocks

Today’s SAF production relies heavily on waste and residue feedstocks -resources that are inherently limited. A broader feedstock base could help the industry scale supply in line with rising demand. Cover crops such as camelina and carinata offer a scalable alternative and can be used with existing HEFA technology that has already been built out.

Grown between existing agricultural cycles, they do not compete with food production and can improve soil health while increasing SAF feedstock supply. While RED III has taken a positive step in recognising these feedstocks, current draft certification rules risk limiting their practical deployment.

A core enabler of this approach for us is integration across the bp group. We work closely with bp’s refining, biofuels and technology teams to support SAF production through refinery co processing at sites such as Lingen in Germany and Castellón in Spain. By processing renewable feedstocks, such as waste oils, vegetable oils and fats, alongside conventional crude (which remains the vast majority of what we process today), co processing offers a cost effective route to increasing SAF volumes while using established assets.

Integration across bp enables SAF to be blended, stored and distributed alongside conventional fuel - reducing cost and complexity while allowing adoption to be accelerated. As a result, we now supply SAF to customers at around 60 locations across 22 countries - a footprint built through steady infrastructure led expansion rather than isolated one off projects.

Where SAF began

Long before SAF formed part of mainstream aviation strategy, our early efforts focused squarely on technical feasibility and safety, as we recognised that no alternative fuel could gain industry acceptance without meeting aviation’s uncompromising standards. As with everything we do at Air bp, safety comes first and performance has been built-in from the ground up.

In those early years, we supported some of the first SAF test flights, working alongside aircraft and engine manufacturers, airlines and regulators to validate performance and fuel integrity. These programmes were rigorous, multi year efforts designed to generate operational evidence rather than symbolic milestones.

title: North American Solvents Outlook 2026: Stocking Cycles Cannot Mask Weak Demand
description:
A temporary inventory-building cycle lifted North American solvent prices, but weak underlying demand and global competition continue to define the market.
Underlying Demand Has Not Materially Improved Demand across coatings, inks, adhesives and general industrial applications remains close to 2025 levels.
Solvents tied more closely to propylene, acetone or imported supply remain more exposed to weak demand and competitive pressure.
H2 Outlook The key question is whether higher energy values trigger another stocking cycle or whether buyers resist because they are still consuming earlier inventories.
Soft demand, overcapacity and uneven recovery suggest that volatility may delay a true solvent-market recovery into 2027 or later.
text:
A temporary inventory-building cycle lifted North American solvent prices, but weak underlying demand and global competition continue to define the market.

Key Takeaways

Demand across coatings, inks, adhesives and general industrial applications remains close to 2025 levels.

End users stocked more aggressively from March through May, supporting sharp price increases across several solvent markets.

Toluene, mixed xylenes and regular mineral spirits have stronger near-term support because of their relationship to crude, gasoline and clean-product values.

Underlying Demand Has Not Materially Improved

Demand across coatings, inks, adhesives and general industrial applications remains close to 2025 levels. Most purchasing is tied to immediate requirements rather than broad inventory rebuilding.

Geopolitical Risk Created a Temporary Margin Opportunity

End users stocked more aggressively from March through May, supporting sharp price increases across several solvent markets. That activity improved supplier margins temporarily, but it did not signal a durable recovery in consumption.

Feedstock Exposure Is Separating Product Performance

Toluene, mixed xylenes and regular mineral spirits have stronger near-term support because of their relationship to crude, gasoline and clean-product values. Solvents tied more closely to propylene, acetone or imported supply remain more exposed to weak demand and competitive pressure.

MEK, IPA and acetone Show Different Correction Paths

MEK recorded the clearest boom-and-correction cycle, rising into the upper $2-per-pound range before some values fell below $1 per pound as sellers cleared inventory ahead of new shipments. IPA moderated more slowly because of US Gulf supply constraints, but freight concessions outside the region indicated weaker effective netbacks. Acetone also weakened as lower propylene costs, adequate supply and slow derivative demand pressured spot values.

H2 Outlook

The key question is whether higher energy values trigger another stocking cycle or whether buyers resist because they are still consuming earlier inventories. Soft demand, overcapacity and uneven recovery suggest that volatility may delay a true solvent-market recovery into 2027 or later.

title: Kazakhstan Considers Oilseed-Based Aviation Fuel Project with Hong Kong Investor
description:
Kazakhstan is considering a plant in Alatau City to produce sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from industrial oilseeds in cooperation with Hong Kong investment firm Full Vision Capital.
Alatau City is a new city near Almaty operating under a special legal regime.
Ukrainian drone attacks have disrupted Russian refineries in 2026, affecting fuel exports to Central Asia.
Jet fuel exports by rail to Central Asia and Afghanistan fell by more than 92% in June from May, while Russia restricted exports of jet fuel and other refined products, Reuters reported.

text:
Kazakhstan is considering a plant in Alatau City to produce sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from industrial oilseeds in cooperation with Hong Kong investment firm Full Vision Capital. Deputy Agriculture Minister Azat Sultanov said at a government meeting on August 4 that the proposal was under consideration. Alatau City is a new city near Almaty operating under a special legal regime.

An industry analysis published on June 18 said Kazakhstan’s three refineries produced about 750,000-760,000 metric tons of aviation kerosene in 2025, while total demand was estimated at 1.2 million tons. The analysis, citing Ministry of Energy data, said domestic production covered the needs of domestic airlines, but international carriers and transit or cargo operations left an overall shortfall of roughly 450,000 tons. Russia has traditionally supplied much of the balance.

Ukrainian drone attacks have disrupted Russian refineries in 2026, affecting fuel exports to Central Asia. Jet fuel exports by rail to Central Asia and Afghanistan fell by more than 92% in June from May, while Russia restricted exports of jet fuel and other refined products, Reuters reported.

Speaking at the cabinet meeting, Sultanov said the government was expanding support for agricultural processing projects that produce higher-value goods.

“To expand exports, including to more distant markets, we are developing deeper processing industries,” Sultanov said. “Alongside major projects producing starches, amino acids, gluten, feed additives and other value-added products, the administration of Alatau City, together with Full Vision Capital, is also considering a project to produce aviation fuel from oilseed crops.”

The August 4 remarks followed discussions held in July. Agriculture Minister Aidarbek Saparov met company representatives on July 9 to discuss SAF production from industrial oilseeds, with agricultural and food waste considered as additional feedstock. A day earlier, Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev met a delegation from Towngas and Full Vision Capital to discuss a possible SAF plant using EcoCeres technology in Alatau City.

Full Vision Capital is the family office of Hong Kong businessman Peter Lee. Its portfolio includes EcoCeres, which produces SAF and hydrotreated vegetable oil. Officials in Kazakhstan have identified Alatau City as a priority location for the proposed plant, which remains under discussion.
